pages.caption: There was once a poor woodcutter who had seven sons, the youngest only seven.
pages.scene: A poor woodcutter and his wife

pages.caption: He was very little, and when born no bigger than one's thumb, which made him
pages.scene: Little Thumb is smaller than a thumb

pages.caption: be called Little Thumb.
pages.scene: Little Thumb is smaller than a thumb

pages.caption: The poor child bore the blame of whatsoever was done amiss in the house, and,
guilty or not, was always in the wrong.
Little Thumb was more cunning and had a far greater share of wisdom than all
his brothers put together.
There happened now to come a very bad year, and the famine was so great
that these poor people resolved to rid themselves of their children.
One evening the fagot-maker said to his wife that he was resolved to lose them
pages.scene: The father speaks of his plan

pages.caption: in the wood to-morrow.
pages.scene: The father speaks of his plan

pages.caption: The wife cried out in horror, but having considered what a grief it would be
to see them perish with hunger, she at last consented.
Little Thumb heard every word that had been spoken, for he got up softly and
hid himself under his father's stool.
He went to bed again, but did not sleep a wink all the rest of
the night,
thinking on what he had to do.
He got up early in the morning and went to the river-side, where he filled
his pockets full of small white pebbles.
They all went abroad, but Little Thumb never told his brothers one syllable of what
pages.scene: The family walks into the forest

pages.caption: he knew.
pages.scene: The family walks into the forest

pages.caption: They went into a very thick forest, where they could not see one another at
ten paces distance.
The fagot-maker began to cut wood, and the children to gather up the sticks to
make fagots.
Their father and mother, seeing them busy at their work, got away from them insensibly
and ran away from them all at once.
When the children saw they were left alone, they began to cry as loud as
they could.
Little Thumb let them cry on, knowing very well how to get home again by
pages.description: [Little Thumb stays calm amid the tears]

pages.caption: means of the little white pebbles he had dropped along the way.
pages.description: [white pebbles gleam on the forest floor]

pages.caption: He said to his brothers that he would lead them home again, only follow him.
pages.scene: Little Thumb leads the brothers home

pages.caption: They did so, and he brought them home by the very same way they came
into the forest.
They dared not go in, but sat themselves down at the door, listening to what
their father and mother were saying.
The very moment the fagot-maker and his wife reached home the lord of the manor
sent them ten crowns, which he had owed them a long while.
This gave them new life, for the poor people were almost famished.
The fagot-maker sent his wife immediately to the butcher's.
When they had eaten, the woman said that she was sorry for their poor children.
She spoke so very loud that the children began to cry out all together: Here
we are.
She ran immediately to open the door and hugged them, saying she was glad to
see her dear children.
They sat down to supper, and ate with such a good appetite as pleased both
father and mother.
The good folks were extremely glad to see their children once more at home.
This joy continued while the ten crowns lasted.
When the money was all gone, they fell again into their former uneasiness and resolved
to lose them again.
Little Thumb got up very early in the morning to go and pick up some
pebbles,
but he found the house-door double-locked.
When their father had given each of them a piece of bread for their breakfast,
Little Thumb fancied he might make use of this instead of the pebbles.
pages.description: [Little Thumb looks at his bread thoughtfully]

pages.caption: He put the bread in his pocket.
pages.scene: He puts the bread in his pocket

pages.caption: Their father and mother brought them into the thickest and most obscure part of the
forest.
Little Thumb thought he could easily find the way again by means of his bread,
pages.description: [Little Thumb drops crumbs along the path]

pages.caption: which he had scattered all along as he came.
But he was very much surprised when he could not find so much as one
pages.description: [Little Thumb searches the ground in vain]

pages.caption: crumb;
the birds had come and eaten it up, every bit.
pages.description: [birds fly away with the last crumbs]

pages.caption: They were now in great affliction, for the farther they went the more they were
out of their way.
Night now came on, and there arose a terribly high wind, which made them dreadfully
afraid.
They fancied they heard on every side of them the howling of wolves coming to
eat them up.
pages.description: [brothers cling to each other in fear]

pages.caption: After this, it rained very hard, which wetted them to the skin.
Little Thumb climbed up to the top of a tree, to see if he could
pages.description: [Little Thumb scrambles up a tall tree]

pages.caption: discover anything.
He saw at last a glimmering light, like that of a candle, but a long
way from the forest.
They came at last to the house where this candle was, not without an abundance
of fear.
They knocked at the door, and a good woman came and opened it.
Little Thumb told her they were poor children who had been lost in the forest,
pages.description: [Little Thumb speaks politely at the door]

pages.caption: and desired to lodge there for God's sake.
The woman, seeing them so very pretty, began to weep and told them this house
belonged to a cruel ogre who eats up little children.
Little Thumb said they would rather the gentleman should eat them than be devoured by
the wolves.
The Ogre's wife let them come in and brought them to warm themselves at a
very good fire.
There was a whole sheep upon the spit, roasting for the Ogre's supper.
As they began to be a little warm they heard three or four great raps
at the door; this was the Ogre.
Upon this she hid them under the bed and went to open the door.
The Ogre presently asked if supper was ready and sat himself down to table.
pages.description: [ogre sits at the head of the table]

pages.caption: He sniffed about to the right and left, saying: I smell fresh meat.
The Ogre said there was something here which he did not understand.
As he spoke these words he got up from the table and went directly to
the bed.
He said he would not eat them up now, but save them for three ogres
of his acquaintance.
The Ogre's wife gave them a good supper, but they were so much afraid they
could not eat a bit.
As for the Ogre, he sat down again to drink, being highly pleased that he
had got wherewithal to treat his friends.
He drank a dozen glasses more than ordinary, which got up into his head and
obliged him to go to bed.
The Ogre had seven daughters, all little children, with little gray eyes, hooked noses, and
pages.description: [seven eerie daughters sleep in a row]

pages.caption: very long sharp teeth.
They had been put to bed early, with every one a crown of gold upon
her head.
Little Thumb observed that the Ogre's daughters had crowns of gold upon their heads.
He got up about midnight and took his brothers' bonnets and put them upon the
pages.description: [Little Thumb tiptoes through the dark room]

pages.caption: heads of the seven little ogresses.
He took off their crowns of gold, which he put upon his own head and
his brothers'.
The Ogre waking about midnight, threw himself hastily out of bed, taking his great knife.
pages.description: [ogre grabs his knife in the dark]

pages.caption: He went up, groping all the way, into his daughters' chamber.
He came to the bed where the little boys lay, and, feeling the golden crowns,
said he should have made a fine piece of work of it.
Then he went to the bed where the girls lay and, having found the boys'
little bonnets,
he cut the throats of all his seven daughters.
Well pleased with what he had done, he went to bed again to his wife.
As soon as Little Thumb heard the Ogre snore, he waked his brothers and bade
them all put on their clothes presently and follow him.
They stole down softly into the garden and got over the wall.
They kept running about all night, and trembled all the while, without knowing which way
they went.
The Ogre, when he awoke, said to his wife to go upstairs and dress those
young rascals.
The wife was strangely astonished when she perceived her seven daughters killed and weltering in
their blood.
The Ogre said the wretches should pay for it, and that instantly.
He threw a pitcher of water upon his wife's face and gave her his boots
pages.description: [ogre throws water and hands over boots]

pages.caption: of seven leagues.
He went out and ran over a vast deal of ground, and came at last
into the very road where the poor children were.
Little Thumb, seeing a hollow rock near the place where they were, made his brothers
pages.description: [Little Thumb points to the hiding place]

pages.caption: hide themselves in it.
The Ogre, who found himself much tired, went to sit down upon the rock where
the little boys had hid themselves.
As it was impossible he could be more weary than he was, he fell asleep
and began to snore so frightfully that the poor children were no less afraid.
Little Thumb told them that they should run away immediately toward home while the Ogre
was asleep.
pages.description: [brothers creep out from under the ogre]

pages.caption: They took his advice and got home presently.
Little Thumb came up to the Ogre, pulled off his boots gently and put them
on his own legs.
pages.description: [boots shrink to fit his tiny feet]

pages.caption: The boots were very long and large, but, as they were fairies, they had the
gift of becoming big and little, according to the legs of those who wore them.
pages.description: [boots change size with a magical glow]

pages.caption: He went immediately to the Ogre's house, where he saw his wife crying bitterly.
Little Thumb told her that her husband was in very great danger, being taken by
a gang of thieves.
The good woman gave him all she had, for this Ogre was a very good
husband.
Little Thumb, having thus got all the Ogre's money, came home to his father's house.
He was received with abundance of joy.
He went to Court, where he was informed that they were in much pain about
a certain army, which was two hundred leagues off.
He went to the King and told him that he would bring him news from
pages.scene: Little Thumb speaks to the king

pages.caption: the army before night.
pages.scene: Little Thumb speaks to the king

pages.caption: The King promised him a great sum of money upon that condition.
Little Thumb was as good as his word, and returned that very same night with
the news.
He got whatever he pleased, for the King paid him very well for carrying his
orders to the army.
After having for some time carried on the business of a messenger, he went home
to his father, where it was impossible to express the joy they were all in.
pages.description: [family embraces him with tears of joy]

pages.caption: He made the whole family very easy, bought places for his father and brothers, and
settled them very handsomely in the world.
